Gravings
GRAY-vingz
n. pl. (engraved work; the cut borders on the bases of the lavers in Solomon's house)
From Old English grafan, to dig or carve. At 1 Kings 7:31 it renders Hebrew miqlaoth, engravings; the related noun pittuach is used of the engravings of a signet on the priestly stones.

Biblical Definition

The description of the ten brazen bases in Solomon's court is one of the most technical passages in Scripture, and it does not skip the underside of the work: and also upon the mouth of it were gravings with their borders, foursquare, not round. These were wheeled stands holding lavers for washing the instruments of sacrifice — utility furniture, standing in the open court, and engraved. Two verses later the record adds cherubim, lions and palm trees graved on the plates and ledges of the same bases, according to the proportion of every one. The Holy Ghost saw fit to preserve the fact that the washstands were beautiful.

The same craft appears in the holiest place the trade could reach. The onyx stones on the high priest's shoulders bore the names of the tribes cut like the engravings of a signet, and the golden plate on his forehead carried two words in the same hand: HOLINESS TO THE LORD. That is what engraving is for in Scripture — permanence. A signet cuts a name into metal so that what is stamped with it cannot be disputed, and the priest went in with the tribes cut into stone on his shoulders and the LORD's holiness cut into gold on his head. When Isaiah wants the strongest possible word for God's memory of His people, he reaches for the same craft: Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): engravings; figures or letters cut into a hard surface with a sharp instrument.

expand to see more

GRAVING, n. The act of carving or cutting figures; carved work; engraving.

GRAVE, v.t. To carve or cut letters or figures on stone or other hard substance; to engrave.

ENGRAVING, n. The act or art of cutting figures or letters on wood, stone or metal.

SIGNET, n. A seal; particularly, a seal used to give authority to a writing.

LAVER, n. A vessel for washing; a large basin used in the temple service.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 7:31 — "And the mouth of it within the chapiter and above was a cubit: but the mouth thereof was round after the work of the base, a cubit and an half: and also upon the mouth of it were gravings with their borders, foursquare, not round."

1 Kings 7:36 — "For on the plates of the ledges thereof, and on the borders thereof, he graved cherubims, lions, and palm trees, according to the proportion of every one, and additions round about."

Exodus 28:11 — "With the work of an engraver in stone, like the engravings of a signet, shalt thou engrave the two stones with the names of the children of Israel: thou shalt make them to be set in ouches of gold."

Exodus 39:30 — "And they made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and wrote upon it a writing, like to the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD."

Modern Corruption

The long technical passages about the temple furniture are skipped as tedious, and with them goes the doctrine that God is particular about how His house is made.

expand to see more

1 Kings 7 is where a great many Bible-reading plans quietly lose their readers, and the loss is not neutral. The chapter exists to record that God specified the dimensions, the metals, the proportion and the ornament of vessels used for washing, and that He preserved the record afterward. That is the regulative principle in narrative form: the house of God is built to His word and not to the builder's taste, down to whether the mouth of a base is foursquare or round. A congregation that has never read the chapter will find it hard to see why Scripture must govern worship in the New Testament too.

There is no significant postmodern redefinition of this word to rebut. The principle to recover is the one the engraver's craft exists to teach: what is cut is permanent. The priest bore the names of the tribes cut into onyx on his shoulders whenever he went in, and Isaiah takes the same trade to make the strongest promise in the prophets — I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands; thy walls are continually before me. An engraving cannot be wiped off. That is why the Holy Ghost chose it for the doctrine of God's remembrance of His elect.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew miqlaoth (H4734), engravings; pittuach (H6603), an engraving as of a signet; chaqaq (H2710), to cut in, to decree.

expand to see more

Hebrew miqlaoth (H4734) — engravings; the cut borders on the mouths of the bases.

Hebrew pittuach (H6603) — an engraving, as of a signet; the word used of the tribal names and the golden plate.

Hebrew chotham (H2368) — a signet, a seal; the standard of permanence the craft appeals to.

Hebrew chaqaq (H2710) — to cut in, to inscribe, and so to decree; Isaiah's word for the graving on God's hands.

Hebrew charash (H2796) — a craftsman in wood, stone or metal; the general word for the trade.

Usage

"“upon the mouth of it were gravings with their borders” — washstands, engraved."

"“like the engravings of a signet” — the standard of permanence."

"“HOLINESS TO THE LORD” — two words cut in gold on the priest's forehead."
